So you need to do these two things in full. And whenever you work with us on the higher side, if you are over 300,000 sessions, we'll do a full comprehensive audit. We'll spend two, three weeks doing that audit and we'll come to you with about a 100page document of our findings around your audience, their wants, their objections, their friction points, their needs. Um, and it will unear so much about your business that you can utilize, not just on site, but on ads, on retention, etc. Um, but even on the lower side, under 300,000 sessions, do those ones that are bolded, non-negotiables. It's going to take you about a week or two to gather the data and then you can make more informed decisions. Speaking of informed decisions, let's have a look at the strategy when it comes to CRO. So, there are three things that we uh we always look for when we're creating a a hypothesis or AB test idea. Basically, one is the change. So, what is what do we plan to alter? Very simple. Two is the expected outcome. Now, we can only have this expected outcome if we actually do our research enough. we do that data analysis enough. So, what's the results that we anticipate? And the rationale again, the data backs the rationale. Why do we believe this is going to change? Well, because all our post-purchase surveys said that people didn't realize how long it would take to get results with the supplement. Therefore, we're going to create a section just below the fold that says this is how quickly you can see results with our supplement. It's very, very simple. Nothing to do with CRO is complicated. It's just putting the pieces of data together and using common sense. It's all around human psychology, user buying psychology, uh, and and that's how you tap into effective CRO. What we do here internally is we will do all that research. We will then create uh a framework here. We use the PXL framework. It's not ours. We're not going to pretend we invented it. It's very, very simple. We'll put it into a leaderboard. So, when you have all your test ideas from that data, uh, you put the test ideas down here. You put a score of one to uh 1 to 10 here. Let's talk about testing before we get into those case studies, guys. Let's talk about testing. Okay, so a few foundational principles. I didn't want to make this too long, but I promised you after 12 years, I really do feel uh a a proper responsibility to show you this stuff first before I just go, "Hey, look at what you can do with CRO because it's not easy. Yes, it's common sense. Yes, you can do it, but it's not easy. You you need to rely on that data. So, typically we're talking here about an AB test, but it could be ABC D. You could be testing three variations. You could be doing multivariate testing. We can talk about that in detail uh shortly. Multivariate testing should only be done at high volume. Um but you have a control which is your current version versus the variation. Whether that's three variations, it doesn't matter. uh statistical significance is is important and a a good CRO testing tool will tell you statistical significance but what's more important is power because what power stat power means is uh it's based on a big enough data set to say that that test is proven to make you more money. Okay. So if a statistical significance is for example flipping a coin three times and two times it landing on heads and then the software going heads is better. It's going to convert way way better because it's statistically significantly more that heads has come up than tails. But what power means is you've done that test enough at enough velocity that you can prove it's actually going to do it. Because if we flip that coin another 10 times it could be tails all the times. So we need to make sure we have enough data set to do that. Um as far as sample sizing, we would always run 50 to 100k sessions through a test. Uh depending on where that test would be. We like to run especially on the comprehensive so over 300,000 sessions test for at least two weeks because we don't want external factors to alter the test. For example, run it two Mondays, two Tuesdays, two Wednesdays, two Thursdays. If your competitor and there's only two of you in the market all of a sudden has a sale on a Monday, your test is going to go down on a Monday and you may make a rash decision, kill the test, but it could have been a winning test. So run it over a couple of weeks just to get it and obviously randomize that test as well. Couple of best practices for you. Um always have a clear hypothesis. So always have a predefined measurable test that you want to do. I think this listical is going to convert better because X Y and Zed. Um try and avoid conflicting tests. If you are doing a velocity of small AB tests, so if you are a high volume store, try to avoid uh doing multiple tests on a PDP at the same time. For example, you can still do like a homepage test and a cart test because they're far apart.
